description: The closing-credits anthem of Fight Club began life on Pixies' 1988 debut album Surfer Rosa — presented here in the band's official lyric video, built around Vaughan Oliver's original 4AD artwork.

pops.text: Black Francis wrote this after snorkeling in Barbados — a little fish kept chasing him, and the surreal lyric swam straight out of that encounter.
It's track seven on Surfer Rosa (1988), Pixies' first full-length album, released on the British indie label 4AD.
Producer Steve Albini recorded the album at Q Division Studios in Boston in about ten days, on a budget of roughly $10,000.
That ghostly 'ooh-ooh' floating over everything is bassist Kim Deal — credited on the album under her joke married name, Mrs. John Murphy.
Albini loved capturing studio chatter, and Surfer Rosa is full of it — he later became famous for the same raw approach with Nirvana's In Utero.
Francis and guitarist Joey Santiago met as students at UMass Amherst; Deal joined after answering a newspaper ad seeking a bassist into Husker Du and Peter, Paul and Mary.
Drummer David Lovering's steady, minimal beat is the anchor — Francis said the song is basically a simple chord sequence anyone could strum, made strange by the delivery.
It was never released as a single in 1988. The song slowly grew into a cult favorite through college radio and word of mouth.
Then came Fight Club (1999): the song plays over the final scene as the towers fall, and a whole new generation adopted it overnight.
Placebo, Nada Surf and countless others have covered it — but nobody else gets that Deal-and-Francis ache quite right.

title: Where Is My Mind?

description: Rhino's official live video catches the Cars in their 1978 breakthrough year, performing the Ric Ocasek song that Boston radio had already turned into a local phenomenon as a demo.

pops.text: Ric Ocasek wrote this in the basement of a commune in Newton, Massachusetts, where he was living before the Cars had a record deal.
The lead vocal isn't Ocasek — it's bassist Benjamin Orr, the band's co-frontman, whose smoother voice fronts several of their biggest hits.
Before it was ever released, the band's demo of this song became the most-requested song by a local act in the history of Boston station WBCN.
Their manager took that demo to two Boston stations, and the airplay helped land the Cars their Elektra Records deal.
Producer Roy Thomas Baker — fresh off Queen's biggest records — gave the debut album its glossy, layered sound at AIR Studios in London.
Elliot Easton's 15-second guitar solo was fully composed before recording: he told Guitar Player that repeated gigging let him zero in on every note in advance.
Listen to the intro — it nods to the Ohio Express bubblegum hit 'Yummy Yummy Yummy' (1968), and the 'time-time' lyric tips a hat to the Velvet Underground's 'Sister Ray.'
Released as the band's first single in 1978, it peaked at #27 on the Billboard Hot 100 and #17 in the UK.
The debut album it came from stayed on the Billboard chart for 139 weeks and eventually went six-times platinum in the US.
Seven years later the song resurfaced as the B-side of 'Tonight She Comes,' the Cars' last Top 10 hit — and it later opened the Oscar-winning film Boys Don't Cry.

title: Just What I Needed

description: Elton's futuristic glam satire from Goodbye Yellow Brick Road finally got an official video in 2017 — a choreographed sci-fi piece by Jack Whiteley and Laura Brownhill, winners of Elton's 'The Cut' video competition.

pops.text: Bernie Taupin's lyric imagines a futuristic, androgynous rock band — a gentle satire of the music business and its manufactured stars.
It was recorded in May 1973 at the Château d'Hérouville in France, the studio mansion where Elton cut much of his classic run.
It sounds live, but it isn't: producer Gus Dudgeon added canned applause and crowd noise in the studio to fake a concert atmosphere.
That stuttering piano intro is Elton vamping in a style he based on old vaudeville and music-hall playing.
Elton's band here is his classic lineup: Davey Johnstone on guitar, Dee Murray on bass and Nigel Olsson on drums.
Elton actually resisted releasing it as a single — he thought it was too weird. In the US, a Detroit DJ's airplay forced the label's hand.
Good call by the DJ: the single topped the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1974, Elton's second US #1.
It crossed over, too — reaching #15 on the Billboard R&B chart, a rare feat for Elton that won him an invitation to perform on Soul Train.
The parent album, Goodbye Yellow Brick Road, is a double LP that spent eight weeks at #1 in America.
This video arrived 44 years after the song: it won 'The Cut,' the 2017 YouTube competition Elton and Taupin ran to give three of their classics their first official videos.

title: Bennie And The Jets

description: Phish's official pro-shot video of the A Picture of Nectar favorite, performed at Saratoga Performing Arts Center on July 3, 2016 — its return after nearly a year on the shelf, synchronized dance included.

pops.text: The song is really three pieces stitched together: 'Guelah Papyrus,' 'The Asse Festival,' and 'Guelah (The Fly)' — they haven't been played separately since their first performances.
Trey Anastasio explained the title live in 1991: Geulah was the mother of his childhood friend Dave Abrahams, who would pull Dave out of his room mid-hangout.
Anastasio wrote the music and Tom Marshall, Phish's longtime lyricist, wrote the words — their partnership dates back to their school days in New Jersey.
It debuted live in February 1991 and became a fixture of 1991–94 setlists before turning into a relative rarity.
The studio version anchors A Picture of Nectar (1992), Phish's major-label debut for Elektra — the album is named for Nectar Rorris, owner of Nectar's, the Burlington bar where Phish cut their teeth.
Watch the instrumental break: Trey and bassist Mike Gordon perform a synchronized little dance, a piece of choreography Phish fans have adored for decades.
A beloved 1998 rendition at Hampton Coliseum was preserved on the live album Hampton Comes Alive.
Trey singled this song out in a Rolling Stone interview as one he wished the band would play more often.
Phish obliged at SPAC on July 3, 2016 — this performance — dusting it off after nearly a year, with drummer Jon Fishman leaving his kit to join the dance.
At the end, Trey and Mike held up their sneakers: an 'H' on his shoe, an 'I' on Gordon's neon-green one — together, 'HI.'

title: Guelah Papyrus

description: The Savannah jam band's Miami Vice-named funk instrumental in its natural habitat: a fan-shot performance from Amberland 2006, Perpetual Groove's own festival, at Deerfields in North Carolina.

pops.text: Yes, the title is exactly what you think: Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs, the pastel-suited detectives of TV's Miami Vice, played by Don Johnson and Philip Michael Thomas.
Perpetual Groove formed in 1997 in Savannah, Georgia — founders Brock Butler and Adam Perry met as freshmen at the Savannah College of Art and Design.
The classic lineup took shape in 2001, when drummer Albert Suttle and keyboardist Matt McDonald — both then active-duty US Army — met Butler and Perry at a Savannah open-mic night.
The studio version is track seven on All This Everything (2004), produced by Robert Hannon — and even on record it runs a jammy 7:13.
Live, it stretches much further: the version on All This Everything (Live) clocks in at 16:11, with the groove opened up for improvisation.
This footage comes from Amberland, the band's own Memorial Day weekend festival — it began as a friends-and-family party on a farm in Jefferson, Georgia.
Amberland was a one-band festival: Perpetual Groove played long sets all weekend, and Butler traditionally played a Sunday-morning acoustic set fans nicknamed Brockfest.
The song is a segue machine — at Amberland 2007 the band famously sandwiched it around 'Robot Waltz': Crockett and Tubbs, into Robot Waltz, back into Crockett and Tubbs.
Bassist Adam Perry is the engine here — at a 2023 Lark Hall show in Albany, reviewers singled out his bass lines on this song as stealing the night and getting the whole room dancing.
It's listed among the band's signature popular songs alongside 'Three Weeks' and 'Stealy Man' — three decades on, it remains a setlist staple whenever PGroove tours.

title: Crockett & Tubbs

description: Annie Lennox plays a high-class prostitute chauffeured by Dave Stewart in Mike Brady's sleek video for the opening track of Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This). The synth-pop single flopped on its first release in 1982, then rode the title track's success to the UK Top 10 when it was re-released in 1983.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) (1983), Eurythmics' second album — but the single arrived first, released by RCA on 8 October 1982.

Both the 7-inch and 12-inch singles were backed by the non-LP track 'Monkey Monkey'; the 12-inch also included 'Let's Just Close Our Eyes,' a synth-heavy reworking of the album's earlier single 'The Walk.'
Annie Lennox wrote the lyric to put opposites together: she said she wanted to capture the dichotomy of love and hatred, because love and hate are so close to each other.

Dave Stewart built the track from eighth notes on a Roland synthesiser and a drum-machine pattern with a repeating sixteenth-note hi-hat, then accented passages with an Omnichord to create an electronic harp sound.

Lennox's lead vocal was completed in one take. Stewart said the track already 'sounded eerily complete' before it — he then added guitar overdubs and recorded grunts and breathing sounds because it 'just seemed like a good idea at the time.'
The video was directed by Mike Brady: Stewart acts as chauffeur for Lennox, who plays the role of a high-class prostitute.
Watch for the signature moment: Lennox removes a curly blonde wig to reveal much shorter red hair, slicked back — not the buzz cut seen in the subsequent 'Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)' video.

That wig removal caused minor controversy in the US, where some viewers mistook Lennox for a male cross-dresser. MTV imposed a blackout during one transmission, and its producers telexed RCA Records asking for a copy of her birth certificate.

First time around it was a flop in Britain: it debuted at #70 in November 1982 and peaked at just #54. Re-released after 'Sweet Dreams' broke through, it reached #6 on the UK Singles Chart in April 1983.

In America it was the album's second single: it entered the Billboard Hot 100 at #81 in September 1983, peaked at #23 that November and spent 13 weeks on the chart — and reached #7 on Billboard's Dance Club Songs chart.

title: Love Is a Stranger

description: Siouxsie's shimmering take on the Beatles' White Album song became the Banshees' biggest UK hit — the official video dates from the band's Robert Smith era.

pops.text: John Lennon wrote the original in Rishikesh, India, in 1968, for Prudence Farrow — Mia Farrow's sister — who was meditating so intensely the Beatles worried about her.
The Beatles' version opened side two of the White Album; Lennon fingerpicked it in a style Donovan taught the band in India.
Siouxsie and the Banshees released their cover as a standalone single on September 23, 1983.
It became the biggest hit of their career, peaking at #3 on the UK Singles Chart.
The guitarist in the band at this moment is Robert Smith of the Cure, who toured and recorded with the Banshees in 1982–84 between Cure albums.
Smith's chiming, chorus-drenched guitar is a huge part of this record's dreamy, underwater feel — very different from the Beatles' folk lullaby.
The core Banshees here: Siouxsie Sioux on vocals, Steven Severin on bass, and Budgie — one of post-punk's most inventive drummers — behind the kit.
The single's success was so big that Geffen added it to the US edition of the band's next album, Hyaena (1984).
Siouxsie later said the song had been a favorite since childhood — the Banshees had been playing it live before they ever recorded it.
For many American listeners, this cover — not the White Album — was their first 'Dear Prudence.' It remains the definitive Banshees single.

title: Dear Prudence

description: Stevie Nicks's mountain-and-mirror meditation, in the beloved live performance from Fleetwood Mac's 1997 reunion concert The Dance that serves as the song's official video.

pops.text: Stevie Nicks wrote this in 1973 in Aspen, Colorado, staring at the Rockies and wondering whether to quit music, go back to school, or keep going with Lindsey Buckingham.
At the time, she was waiting tables and cleaning houses to support them — their Buckingham Nicks album had flopped and been dropped by its label.
Months later, Mick Fleetwood heard Buckingham Nicks and invited Buckingham to join Fleetwood Mac. He agreed only if Nicks came too. They joined on New Year's Eve 1974.
The song appeared on the band's self-titled 1975 'White Album' — the new lineup's debut, which eventually topped the US chart.
That's Buckingham's delicate fingerpicked guitar under Nicks — no drums, no bass swell, just the two of them, exactly as they'd started.
It was never released as a single in the '70s. It became a standard anyway, through FM radio and a million late-night listens.
The Smashing Pumpkins' acoustic cover (1994) became a US alternative hit and earned Nicks's public praise — she said she was flattered a new generation found it.
This performance is from The Dance (1997), the classic lineup's reunion — Nicks introduces it as a dedication to her father, Jess Nicks.
The live version was finally released as a single in 1998 and charted — more than two decades after the song was recorded.
The Chicks took it back into the US Top 10 in 2002. Rolling Stone ranks 'Landslide' among the 500 greatest songs of all time.

title: Landslide

description: Hancock's 16-bar blues standard in its second famous life: the funk-drenched 1973 Head Hunters remake, which opens with percussionist Bill Summers blowing across beer bottles.

pops.text: Hancock wrote this remembering his Chicago childhood: the cry of the watermelon vendor, and his wagon's wheels beating a rhythm on the cobblestones.
The original appeared on Takin' Off (1962), Hancock's debut album for Blue Note — he was just 22 years old.
That first version is a hard-bop record featuring Freddie Hubbard on trumpet and Dexter Gordon on tenor saxophone, cut at Rudy Van Gelder's studio.
Underneath the melody, it's essentially a 16-bar blues — one reason every young jazz player learns it.
The famous twist: Hancock was filling in for Chick Corea in Mongo Santamaria's band at a Bronx club when, urged by Donald Byrd, he played the tune — and the crowd got up and danced.
Santamaria recorded it on December 17, 1962, and his Latin-pop version hit #10 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1963 — later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
Eleven years later Hancock rebuilt it completely for Head Hunters (1973) — you're hearing that funk version now.
The opening sound is percussionist Bill Summers blowing across beer bottles, imitating hindewhu, the whistled singing of Ba-Benzélé pygmies.
In this remake, saxophonist Bennie Maupin states the famous melody on soprano sax over Paul Jackson's bass and Harvey Mason's drums.
The tune has been recorded more than 200 times — a genuine jazz standard, written before its composer could legally rent a car.

title: Watermelon Man

description: Steel Pulse's daily-devotion anthem from True Democracy, performed live at the Martha's Vineyard Festival on August 10, 2008, in Music Vault's official concert footage.

pops.text: Steel Pulse formed in 1975 in Handsworth, Birmingham, England — school friends who became Britain's most important roots reggae band.
The band's name came from a racehorse: Steel Pulse was a stud whose name the founders spotted and adopted.
'Chant a Psalm' opens True Democracy, released in May 1982 — the band's first album for Elektra Records in America.
The lyric is a Rastafari daily practice set to music: chant a psalm a day to keep the devil away, drawing directly on the Psalms.
Frontman David Hinds, the band's chief songwriter and guitarist, has led Steel Pulse from Handsworth school halls to the world's festival stages.
True Democracy also carries fan favorites 'Your House' and 'Blues Dance Raid' — it remains one of the band's most beloved albums.
Steel Pulse made history in 1986 when their album Babylon the Bandit won the Grammy for Best Reggae Album — the first non-Jamaican band to win it.
This performance was filmed August 10, 2008, at the Martha's Vineyard Festival in Massachusetts — the band more than 30 years into its career.
The song never left the live repertoire: it still turns up in Steel Pulse setlists on tour in the 2020s.
True Democracy got a limited 40th-anniversary vinyl reissue in 2022 — just 500 copies, in a yellow, red and green splatter pressing.

title: Chant a Psalm

description: The Chili Peppers' haunted 6/8 ballad from Blood Sugar Sex Magik — Stephane Sednaoui's surreal official video, and the only Peppers video era with guitarist Arik Marshall in John Frusciante's place.

pops.text: Anthony Kiedis wrote the lyric about his own pattern of leaving relationships — specifically his turbulent on-and-off romance with Carmen Hawk.
It's a ballad in 6/8 time, a real oddity in the Chili Peppers' funk-metal catalog — drummer Chad Smith built the groove from Mitch Mitchell's playing on Hendrix's 'Manic Depression.'
The album, Blood Sugar Sex Magik (1991), was produced by Rick Rubin and recorded at The Mansion in Los Angeles — the same house where Houdini once lived, legend says.
Hear that clattering percussion break? The band raided a junkyard: Flea beat a big pipe, Smith played car brake drums, and Kiedis banged a garbage can.
John Frusciante's acoustic guitar and Mellotron give the song its woozy, medieval shimmer — he was 21 during the sessions.
Released as the album's fourth single on August 3, 1992, it reached #15 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart and #41 in the UK.
By the time this video was shot, Frusciante had quit the band mid-tour in Japan, overwhelmed by fame. He doesn't appear in it.
The guitarist you see is Arik Marshall, Frusciante's short-term replacement — this is one of only two Chili Peppers videos featuring him.
Director Stephane Sednaoui, who also made 'Give It Away,' shot the band against a surreal desert-dreamscape of flowing fabrics and strange figures.
Blood Sugar Sex Magik sold more than 13 million copies worldwide — and this uneasy ballad is the quiet heart of it.

title: Breaking the Girl

description: Paul Simon with Ladysmith Black Mambazo on the Graceland jewel he co-wrote with Joseph Shabalala — a poor boy, a rich girl, and the most joyful walking blues ever recorded.

pops.text: That opening a cappella passage is Ladysmith Black Mambazo singing in Zulu — Simon said he wanted the song to feel like a doorway into the album's world.
Simon co-wrote the song with Joseph Shabalala, Ladysmith's founder — Shabalala shares the songwriting credit, unusual generosity for a Western pop star of the era.
It's from Graceland (1986), the album Simon made after falling for a cassette of South African township music and traveling to Johannesburg to record.
The groove is mbaqanga, South African township pop — Simon built his melody and story-song over the local musicians' rhythms.
Also in the band on this track: Senegalese singer-percussionist Youssou N'Dour and American saxophonist Lenny Pickett.
The story is pure Simon: a rich girl and a poor boy meet in New York, and her wealth is so complete she wears diamonds where nobody would ever look.
Simon and Ladysmith performed the song on Saturday Night Live in November 1986 — a landmark prime-time introduction of South African music to America.
The following year they performed it in Zimbabwe on the Graceland tour, documented in the film The African Concert.
Released as a single in April 1987, it became one of the album's signature tracks, even without a big chart run.
Graceland won the Grammy for Album of the Year and has sold more than 16 million copies — and this track is its closing argument for joy.

title: Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes

description: Springsteen's make-or-break anthem — the official video, directed by Arthur Rosato in 1987, is built from the E Street Band's thunderous 1985 stadium performances of the song.

pops.text: Springsteen wrote this in 1974 on an upright piano in a cottage in Long Branch, New Jersey — starting, as he tells it, with just the title and a guitar riff.
He spent six months recording this one song, layering guitars, keyboards and Clarence Clemons's saxophone into his own Wall of Sound, a deliberate homage to Phil Spector.
The track was cut at 914 Sound Studios in Blauvelt, New York, with producers Mike Appel and, joining midway, critic-turned-manager Jon Landau.
The piano is David Sancious and the drums are Ernest 'Boom' Carter — this was their last session with the band before both left in August 1974.
The 'tramps like us' in the lyric are Romeo-and-Juliet runaways: the narrator, his girl Wendy, and a Jersey Shore town 'that rips the bones from your back.'
An early mix was sent to radio in late 1974 — Cleveland DJ Kid Leo played it relentlessly, building the legend a full year before the album existed.
The album arrived August 25, 1975, and by October Springsteen was on the covers of Time and Newsweek in the same week.
The single peaked at #23 on the Billboard Hot 100 — modest numbers for a song now treated as an American standard.
This video came 12 years later, in 1987, cut from 1984–85 Born in the U.S.A. tour footage and ending with a simple message: 'Thanks to all our fans.'
The recording has been selected for the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry, preserved as a cultural treasure. Baby, this town — and this song — lasts forever.

title: Born To Run

description: The Ramones sit perfectly still at a cafeteria table while chaos erupts around them at double speed — Bill Fishman's official video, made a full decade after the song for the Ramones Mania compilation.

pops.text: Joey Ramone wrote it out of pure boredom: the band was stuck in a London hotel over Christmas 1977, when the whole city shut down — 'nothing to do, nowhere to go.'
It opens side two of Road to Ruin (1978), the Ramones' fourth album, produced by Tommy Ramone and Ed Stasium.
Road to Ruin was the first album with drummer Marky Ramone, who replaced Tommy — Tommy stayed on behind the mixing desk instead.
Marky has said the band deliberately chased the sound of '60s British Invasion groups like the Searchers and the Kinks — maximum melody, minimum fuss.
The songwriting credit is shared by Joey, Dee Dee and Johnny Ramone — all three, on one of their most durable songs.
It was first released not as an A-side but as the B-side of 'She's the One' in September 1978. Marky says he knew from rehearsing it that it couldn't fail.
It reached a wider audience in the 1980 film Times Square, and opened the band's 1988 greatest-hits set, Ramones Mania.
This video was shot for Ramones Mania in 1988, directed by Bill Fishman — the band sits deadpan at a table while nuns, acrobats and chaos swirl around them in fast motion.
The joke is perfect: a song begging to be sedated, performed by four men barely moving a muscle.
Rolling Stone has placed it on its list of the 500 greatest songs of all time — 'twenty, twenty, twenty-four hours to go' is now permanent rock history.

title: I Wanna Be Sedated

description: Earth, Wind & Fire's eternal party-starter in its official HD video — Maurice White and company in full late-'70s regalia, asking the most famous date question in pop: do you remember the 21st night of September?

pops.text: Guitarist Al McKay brought in the looping chord progression; Maurice White and songwriter Allee Willis built the song on it over about a month.
This was Allee Willis's first collaboration with the band — she got the call from Maurice White and went on to co-write much of the I Am album.
Willis kept asking what 'ba-dee-ya' meant. White's answer: never let the lyric get in the way of the groove. The nonsense syllables stayed forever.
And the famous date? Willis has said September 21 was chosen simply because it sang the best of the dates they tried — the 1st, 4th and 9th all lost.
The song was a brand-new track recorded for a greatest-hits package, The Best of Earth, Wind & Fire, Vol. 1 (1978).
Released as a single in November 1978, it peaked at #8 on the Billboard Hot 100 and spent a week at #1 on the R&B chart.
In Britain it went even bigger relative to the band's profile, reaching #3 — it has since been certified multi-platinum there.
That's the Phenix Horns cutting through the groove — Earth, Wind & Fire's horn section was as much a signature as Maurice and Philip Bailey's voices.
Every September 21, the internet celebrates 'Earth, Wind & Fire Day' — comedian Demi Adejuyigbe's annual charity videos built a modern holiday around this song.
It has been added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry — the ba-dee-ya is officially preserved American heritage.

title: September
